transcript.text: My clock shows 07:00. At this point, I'd like to call the regular meeting of the Andover Planning and Zoning Commission to order. For roll call tonight, I see Anne Cremay, Scott Persson, Steve Nelson, and myself as regular members. I see alternates Anne Blanchard, Kevin Arneson, and Susan Englund. And according to my listing, Leanne did tell me that she would probably not be able to join us tonight. And so, next up for the alternates is Anne Blanchard. So, I will seat you in place of Leanne. Sounds good.

Next up is additions or changes to the agenda. Does anybody have any additions or changes to discuss? And I had one. If time allows, and I think it will, I'd like to add new item 7C under new business, the annual report for the Planning Zoning Commission. Any other items to add or change? Hearing none, I'll make a motion to add discussion of the annual report as new business item seven, Charlie. I'll second that.
Thank you, Scott. Any discussion? Hearing none, I'll call for a vote. Anne Cremay? Aye.

Scott? Aye. Steve? Aye. Anne Blanchard? Aye. And I vote aye as well. The motion passes 500. Next up is public comment. I do see that we have a couple members of the public here tonight. Elaine Buchart, you just joined us. Do have anything for us at this point? No. Thanks. Just listening to the POCD discussion.
Okay. And I think I see Catherine Hutchinson. Do you have any comments worse at this point, Ms. Hutchinson? Not at this point.
Okay. If I could be allowed to comment during the gravel pit discussion, please. Absolutely. And
I guess that's next up, moving on to old business. First topic up is the gravel pit discussion, and I will turn that over to Agent Halsey at this point.

Yes. In the minutes, you indicated that I would meet with the owner of Bill Genevieve and his engineer, Chris Bell, on the August 16. That did not happen. It happened later, following week. And I did not make a lot of progress. I tried to skip to the plan, and Bill, the owner, was arguing why another approach is better. Specifically, you don't want to put the low man and was okay with the way the water drained. And I followed up with a letter she was posting basically reiterating what I maintained at that meeting. And Chris Bell submitted a letter, with really a request for a revision plan, eliminating the installation of any additional tile soil and changes to the drainage pattern. I have no further, I mean, this point, the only suggestion I'd have is to approach Mark Bratz, where to go with it, whether he thinks it's appropriate to call a bond, whatever. He's not here to bring it in.

Okay. I don't know if any of the Commission members had the opportunity to see the letter. I just sent it out this afternoon. I think Jim only got it yesterday. So apologize for the late send out on that, but it was sort of a short letter. I can call it up. Well, can try and call it up on screen if we haven't seen it. But essentially, they don't want to put in any topsoil. They think the vegetative growth is good. And he is saying that his as built drawing, although different than what was approved, results in 15% less water drainage to the area on the right hand side of the property. And since based on the discussion that we had when we approved the restoration plan back in August 2022, there was supposed to be no water draining onto property to the right. I don't see how you can reduce that by 15%. But anyhow, at this point, I'll ask if any of the commission members have any questions for Jim about where we are on that.

I I looked at the Asbil that he sent over. There's only really one section there that drains over to the right, and it's a it's a very small section and it drains towards the river, actually. It's not supposed to be draining that way, but I'm saying that it's a very small area that does drain towards.

Agree. It's also not realistic say no water would drain towards towards the south. Right. Exactly. The whole road, which is essentially in the flood floods low flood grid flood zone, which really can't be touched. And the the Ann Arbor Post that that follows that road up back.
It it looks like it's only 30 or 40 feet that drains towards the river. But Yeah. None of it's supposed to.
Well, it's a bridge that's set back from the the Haul Road. Mhmm. There's an area probably 20 feet along that road for for much of it.
Any other thoughts on that, Scott? No. Any other commission members have any comments for Jim at that point? Are you okay with how it is? Who are you asking that to, Scott? Jim. Jim.

I like, I mean, the commission did represent that water would flow certain ways so that, I mean, that would have to be a revision, or a minor correction, which is, I think, very appropriate. As far as the topsoil, I don't see bringing in four inches topsoil for that parcel. I do want to see stabilization. I did request permission to walk the property. I've had some issues in the past, a little volatility. And I did just recently ask permission to walk, take a look at what is on-site as far as stabilization, what has, what seed has taken. I mean, it's sparse. Whether it's going to hold or not, I can't tell. Now, what you would like to see?
Quite honestly, I was hoping that he would come up with some sort of compromise. Don't think his revised proposal was much of a compromise. You got to get him off of something. Right.

The other thing to keep in mind for everybody, and again, I'm not sure that the drainage I guess the problem I have with the drainage is in the email that Jim got that had the response letter in it. He has a drawing that's marked approved 08/15/2022 restoration plan. Yeah, If I can address that Oh, sorry.
But go ahead, Jim. Go ahead and address that then.

Chris Bell submitted with his letter a plan that was different than the approved plan and alluded to it as the approved plan and was posted as such. I was hoping that that was, I tried to correct that. I'm not sure how that worked out, but honestly, I didn't, that was just, I just recently did that and it may have created further confusion. So

we don't need to get into it in too much detail tonight. But if you go back in the archive, the one all the way at the bottom is the gravel pit, I think that's about the first application that we started archiving electronically. And it's got a restoration plan, eightfifteentwenty two, that we approved at a meeting. Subsequent to that, Chris Bell sent and that showed the high point being essentially right at the edge of where it drops off down to the roadway so everything would run back towards the center into a little detention pond. He submitted something that talked about the approved plan later on, And we relabeled that in the archive to the non approved plan of eightfifteentwenty two. That's the one that has a high point ridge somewhere more towards the center of the property than at the edge where it slopes off and has drainage arrows going both ways. So that was not the approved diagram. And I don't know what made him think that was until he submitted it. Some point later, that was the first time I had ever seen that thing, and we had talked about that at the time.

And then he put in the as built, which I didn't really compare in all that detail because I thought it had, I just didn't know of any basis for assuming there'd be 15% less drainage. Now there could have been for what he wrote is the approved plan, but in my mind that was never the approved plan because the approved plan that we talked about in August 15 was a plan that had all arrows running towards the center. And the west side of the boundary was supposed to be at an elevation lower than the east side so that if the detention basin filled in, it would overflow to the west and drain back to the river that way. So this to my point, this is just another poke in the eye that I can understand Mr. Genovese's desire to not bring in a bunch of topsoil, but I don't see any topsoil out there on the lot now. I'm not exactly sure. I got a guess of what happened to

the topsoil that was in the storage area. I think that's buried under the new fill that he had to put down to raise it up to the proper elevation. But nothing has gone according to the plan that he presented and we approved since this project started. And I just don't think that's the standard that we can allow to be acceptable. Anyhow, that's my thought on that. And so I think Jim is reaching out to Mark Grant at this point. And I do not necessarily want to be punitive, but I don't know what the right answer is out there. There's some spots that probably need some topsoil. I acknowledge there's some vegetation that's growing out there. Looks pretty sparse to me on the different times I've been out there. But we have certainly not he has not complied with his plan that we approved, and I got a bit of a problem with that. So I think Jim's on the right course. And we have certainly been over backwards to try and
suit him. Ms. Hutchinson, I know you have been patiently following this saga for the last four years. Any comments for us this evening?
I agree with you that everything that you said with regard to the approved plan. And I also agree that now would be the time to turn it over to Mark Brantz.

Yeah. I know he was supposed to have been complete with the restoration plan last May. We delayed till September with mid September being you know, he's got to have grass seed down about now if we wanted to get anything to germinate before the end of the year and be sure that it got a good start. And it has not. So I'm not sure where to go. Might need some engineering help on the best way to get out of this at this point, but the next step is to engage our land use attorney. And that's what Jim's doing. Okay. Any other comments from anybody on the gravel pit? When did Jim contact Mark?
I just let him know that I shared with him Chris Bell's response plan, which I just got. I was waiting for that
He's see the a fairly aggressive fellow. He'll hop on that. Jim and I just went over the response we got from Chris Bell today, that was the appropriate thing to do. Right. Okay.

Okay. At that point, I'm going to move down to old business 6B, which is proposed revisions to the zoning regulations. And I wanted to talk in general about a couple of things here, one of which was we had talked a couple of times about the accessory dwelling unit, accessory apartments, that sort of thing. And I thought I was zeroing in on what I considered a reasonable approach for the commission to take a look at. I sent that off to Mark Branch, and one of his comments was that he continues to strongly encourage towns to make accessory dwelling units affordable housing, which is a deed restricted thing for 10 as opposed to forty years, which a house would have. Being not the smartest guy in the world on how all the housing things work, I said, Okay, well, that's pretty easy. All that means is that we have to rent restrict what can be charged.

And I think that's well below the threshold for what you would charge for an accessory apartment anyhow. I think an accessory apartment would be affordable in terms of what you get there. So last month, when I was meeting with Eric and John, and I was discussing the plan, John's comment, his feedback was, well, you might be discouraging people from building accessory apartments because There's paperwork that you have to do to document that the people going in are eligible for affordable housing. And that was a new thought to me. I never considered the fact that we would have to restrict who can rent the accessory dwelling unit to those people. My experience in each of the accessory apartments that we've approved so far is that they were all for family members. Right.

And we made arrangements so that when the family member, no longer needed the apartment, it could be rented out. But I didn't recognize the burden on the property owner of going through that. So, I went back to Mark Branch and said, Mark, what do you know about this? Is this the way it works? How does it work? How do you implement that plan? And he said, well, most towns have a housing authority that tracks all that stuff. And we don't have that, so it would be something for Jim to do. And I'll ask John to chime in later on if he's got any experience with any other towns. But Mark Grants' bottom line comment was, are you going to do something about affordable housing or not? And if people want to make an accessory dwelling unit, accessory apartment, and the only way to do that is affordable, then they will probably sign up to that. I was thinking, you know, I looked to the future. At some point, I might want to go into an accessory apartment living at one of my kids' houses. And fortunately, I wouldn't meet the income requirement that's required to live there. And I said, maybe that's not the way we want to go here. But we could probably go either way in the It's not like we're building a ton of these things, but I was trying to get looking for some feedback from the commission members on whether they thought still requiring affordable requiring an accessory apartment to be affordable was the right way for us to go in

an effort to try and make some headway on the affordable housing. And John, before I open it up to the Commission, did you have anything to add? Do you have any experience on managing the admin in there?

Yeah, a little bit. I mean, I've worked with a couple of towns. And again, I mean, Mark France is correct that there's usually an established administrative procedure for this housing authority, which goes through and does annual income verification. But it a burden because in order for those accessory units to count towards the town's eight thirty gs list, its goals toward the 10% state threshold, it does need to be accounted for on an annual basis. So you need to go through those income verification procedures and basically get the tax returns of the tenant, which is kind of a hassle. And most affordable housing landlords or housing authorities sort of have someone that's job is to do that. So, I mean, I think it's worth stepping back and just saying, what is the goal here? Is the goal to promote accessory apartments in general, or to try to leverage accessory apartments specifically as a way to make progress towards the state 10% goal. And if it is that latter thing, the towards the state goal, then we should think about assisting or providing some sort of incentive to those people that are gonna restrict their unit. Because, again, not only is there an administrative burden,

but restricting it to those people that are in the lower income bracket means that you will be restricted in what you can rent the thing for. So in theory, you're foregoing some rent, some percentage of market rent. So it's a little bit of insult to injury. So if you're trying to encourage people to do this, should at least try to make it easier for them to do so.

Now it's my impression that whatever rent we would charge for the small unit there is well below the threshold of what somebody making 80% of the median income would be. I know when we did our study, we said somebody on that income could afford to buy a $300,000 house. I figured the rent for any accessory dwelling unit would be well below what you would pay on a four bedroom home. So I don't know that you're giving up rent per se. And again, I was thinking that in most cases, it starts out being housing for a family member, either just starting out or just ending up. But I would hate to preclude somebody from being able to take advantage of that kind of a deal because
we can't go through the admin that is required to provide that help to our family members if we chose to do so. I have a question. Yep, go ahead, Anne. If

you go through and make this the affordable thing, does that mean that somebody can't build an accessory apartment for their family member if it's not affordable? I mean, like, we have an in law apartment on our house and we built it not because the in laws couldn't afford a bigger house. It's just that we wanted them close by for being able to help them to prevent going into an assisted living or a nursing home. So, that's why we built it not because it had to be affordable. Would that prohibit building that kind of an in law accessory apartment?

Certainly for the way we were proposing the accessory apartment thing, it would. It just says all accessory apartments will be affordable having ten year rent restrictions on it. Ann, your situation was exactly what I was looking at to say, that was a wonderful plan you had, and would we do that? Now, sounds like John was going to disagree with me there, so I'll go back to him so he can make us all smarter on how we might choose to get around that.

No, sorry, Jed, you're correct. I had forgotten that that's what was on the table was mandating that if you do an accessory apartment, it needs to be restricted. So yeah, if that regulation goes in place or is in place, then Jed's answer is correct. I think what I meant to say is it certainly doesn't need to be that way.

But it gets back to providing an incentive for a guy to put the rent restriction in there, and I wasn't sure how to do that. So anyhow, the bottom line at this point is that's why I'm not bringing the accessory apartment thing that I thought was very close back to you guys is it ran off the rails here within the last month, and I haven't figured out how to get it back on the track yet. So no more discussion on that.

Can I make a possible suggestion? Sure. Go ahead, Eric. Is that you leave yourself an out and you say that as of right, you can build accessory dwelling units in all residential zones as, but they have to be affordable housing. By special permit, you can build one and have it not be affordable housing. That way you put the burden on them prove why they want to not do it as affordable housing. If they want to just do it, it's automatically affordable housing. If they want to argue with you about it, maybe you allow them to do it some other way.

Okay. I like that thought. And I'll take that back and try to build that in for what we're looking at there. Because that's the kind of solution I would you know, I'm looking for is that provide some incentive, and I don't know what that would be, or provide an out. And maybe the incentive is you don't have to do the paperwork of going through a special permit. That might be incentive enough for some people to make it affordable. What does John think about that? John, do want to comment?

I'm sorry. What do I think of what I think of Eric's Of what Eric's suggestion was. Yeah. No. And again, I I think that's if if this commission is of the mindset that you want to do what you can to use accessory apartments as a mechanism for doing more to meet the state threshold, then I think Eric's suggestion is a good one. That, you know, the low hanging fruit, which is to say the as of right, you know, administrative zoning permit would be the restricted unit. And if you want to avoid that, then you would go through a more complicated process of a special permit. So that puts the incentives in the right place. And it doesn't outright prohibit someone like Anne from doing a unit, you know, an unrestricted unit for a family member.
Right. Yeah. That sounds like a good idea to me too.

Seems like it still discourages people from doing accessory dwelling units. I think it would be better if there was a way to incentivize people to do the affordable housing without putting a burden on them to go through a special permit process if they don't want to do that. There John, do you have any experience with that where there's incentives that we can offer?

Yes. So there's a couple of incentives that could be considered. I'm just giving examples here. I'm not necessarily advocating to spell something specifically for Andover, but some municipalities have considered providing a tax abatement that essentially that the added value of the property or that accessory unit, you know, they add whatever increased value, you know, would be taxable could be abated or the town could offer a tax, you know, rebate or incentive of a couple $100 or something like that a year to do this. And if the town had administrative resources, and this is done primarily by larger towns or towns with a more robust administrative staff or a housing authority, is to basically offer to help people do that paperwork every year. So basically to eliminate those pain points.

I think those are good ideas. I like the tax abatement issue. If somebody goes affordable housing, that's an incentive. I think it's less you know, the approach for it take taking is, I think, more punitive and discourages people from creating accessory dwelling units. I think if you do the tax abatement, it's more of an incentive approach, carrot versus a stick.

I'm not sure, Steve, that, again, I think the rents on most accessory dwelling units are low enough that they meet the threshold for affordable housing right off the bat. It's only a question of getting out of that admin of verifying that your tenant meets the threshold to go in there. And maybe I didn't dig a lot into the tax incentives because I don't think we've got the staff. And I thought that was clearly something that's not in Jim's thing to do. I don't know. I guess I go back to Eric. You know, Eric, does the town have the wherewithal to manage a tax incentive? I know we're trying to get the tax rules up, not down, but we do you know, I always like carrots more than sticks.

I think you would have a tough time convincing the Board of Selectmen that that was an appropriate venue. They've been pretty reticent to allow tax incentives, which is why we have no PA four ninety for farmers in Andover. Yep. So would they do it for affordable housing? You would have to make a really great case for it, And then you might get them to agree to it. But that would be a discussion between the zoning commission and the Board of Select. That's certainly not anything I could influence on.

Okay. Well, we'll consider that. My thought was pretty much in line with Eric that there's a lot of tax incentives that we're not doing, and that's what's going to make the affordable housing thing a tough nut for us to crack as we get into it more. But accessory dwelling units certainly will continue to add to the role of natural affordable housing. We just don't get any credit for it. And so is natural affordable housing good? Yes, I think it is. Is it too bad that we don't get A credit? I wish there was a way we could do that too, because it's certainly easier to just go out and let the market dictate those smaller rents for smaller houses and apartments. Anything else on accessory apartments at this point? The other thing that I just wanted to mention under this item here was, I think it was either last meeting or the meeting before Eric briefed us on a desire to change the sign regulations and the lighting regulations.

We're talking about lighting up some athletic fields and that sort of thing and maybe putting some banners over on the fence around the track, and at the same time allowing the banners at the school to be hung higher than 10 feet. I was out for quite a bit of the month since the last meeting here, and so I asked Eric not to submit that one because I didn't want that clock to start yet. But I'd be happy to entertain a petition to change the regulations from Eric at the next meeting and get that show on the road. I have given it some thought. I do have the biggest thing that I was concerned with and Eric did exactly what I asked him to do was go out and provide an input so I understand what it is that you're looking to do. The input certainly would take care of anything that the Board of Selectmen wanted to do. My concern was it gave too much latitude to the Board of Selectmen, took too much away from being looked at by the Planning and Zoning Commission. So, I'm trying to put some kind of guardrail in there that keeps us from making a public interest sign that's

100 feet by 100 feet or something someplace. And certainly, you don't think you would do that, but every time you have a strategy that starts out, I hope they don't do that, that strategy never lasts very long. So we got to put something in there. I haven't figured out exactly how to go about that yet. But rather than hash that out here tonight, I just wanted to let the Commission know that we can expect to be seeing that from Eric at the next meeting, and I should be ready to provide a little bit of counter to his offer and seeing how the Commission wants to go on that. And if the Commission wants to go with exactly the way you put it in there, that's all fine and well too. But I want to make sure that we at least discuss having some protections against some wild and crazy ideas that could come at some point down the road. So, any questions on that one? Okay, that gets us to new business. First item up is John with the recap and discussion of the Planet Conservation and Development Survey.

Okay. So first things first, I want to thank everyone both on this commission and some of the other economic development or conservation who went ahead and helped out with the survey, completing the survey online. Whoever is the host, I don't know if it's Jed or the town, if you could allow for screen sharing. I'll go ahead and put the summary on. Everyone has seen the survey itself. But basically, at the end of the 2015 plan, there are two pages that sort of go through the 40 or so implementation. Go ahead and share?
John wants to share? Yes, please. Okay. Hold on one second. Go ahead and try, John.
There we go. Thank you. So hopefully people can see that on the screen. I can make it a little bit shorter, smaller so it fits. Can people see that pretty well? Yep.

Yeah. All right. So these are the final two pages in the plan of conservation and development, which is sort of an implementation task summary. I forwarded this around this afternoon, so people hopefully got a chance to see it. And so based on the results of the survey, which again, here, it was a fairly lengthy survey, 48 questions or 48 implementation tasks. And people were asked to comment on the progress and relevance of the action steps that were identified in the 2015 Plan of Conservation and Development. Each question identified one of the action steps. And in this case, the first one was the the to do list item was adopt the Andover Rural Design Regulation, the ARD. And the options were, you know, is this task that we're supposed to do over the ten year cycle complete? Not complete, but still important. Not complete, but its relevance has sort of diminished. Not sure of of where it stands, but it's still a relevant thing,

and then just straight not sure. And so I I went through responses. In the case of ARD, people were fairly confident, significantly so, that it had been completed and could be sort of checked off the list. And then there were a number of others that, let's see, I'm sort of scrolling through. So like I'm making an open space plan that's easily available to developers and landowners. Some people believe it was in progress. Some people believe it was not complete, and those two could be the same, but it's still relevant. And so what I basically looked for through this survey, again, 48 tasks, was to sort of sort through and identify those items that either were generally by consensus found to be primarily complete or those things that were incomplete and in progress, but still very important. So I've sorted through this list. The blue check marks essentially mean that significant progress has been made or the items are believed to be complete. And I would certainly look to this commission, look to Eric to sort of ground truth those. And then the orange stars were those items that were listed as incomplete or hadn't really gotten underway,

but were still very relevant and important to as a task to carry forward. And, Jen, I'll also note we we received sort of a commentary from the Economic Development Commission about these items, and I've incorporated their comments on the task that they've undertaken, and particularly on the second page where we look at Andover Town Center and creating an identity and sense of place, a number of those economic development things and actually, well, it's probably on the promoting of regulated commercial development. A number of those elements in terms of working with property owners and encouraging economic development. I incorporated their comments there as well. Jed, I will leave it to you if you want me to go through some of the things that people believed were relatively complete,
but I think this is a pretty decent summary of where people felt like the town ended up and things that were still important to focus on going forward.

Okay. So I know Elaine is with us tonight. And my thought I spoke with Hank Gruner over the course of the last month with the chapter eight on the conservation stuff and told him that I thought what we would be doing was saving the conservation and economic development to next month to invite them all after we had a chance to see how the other sections went and that way not have them sit through a whole thing here. Elaine, you're here tonight. Would you prefer to discuss the economic development topics tonight, or would you prefer to hold those off until next month where you can have some other members join you? Or you think asking them to attend another meeting is just too much to hope for and you're going to take the message back to them?
Well, I'm just going to take the message back to them. Okay. Mean, them is Kathy Palazzi. There's only two of us left, Yep.

Okay. Sounds good. So, John, with that, I think if you could go through, we'll save the natural resources thing for next month, and we'll try to work our way through the rest of them here tonight, seeing how that goes.

Okay. So we'll sort of buzz through these a little bit and we can pause for some comment. So the first several, and I'll tell them we'll go up here, and this is chapter seven, Managing Future Growth, making this a little bigger. The priorities were adopting the Andover Rural District, which people believed were primarily done. Rezoning areas of R40 to R80, and I'll toggle back and forth here, commentary, there was a lot of uncertainty. You know, some people believed it was done and maybe the people sort of on the inside of planning and zoning discussions, but most people weren't really sure where we are. Well, and I knew this would have some

variance in answers because we didn't go to R40 or R80. We made all the R40s in the 1960s. And so there was probably some lack of understanding of how to answer that one best. But I do think we rezoned everything to a common zoning. Why we chose 60 instead of 80, not exactly sure. Eric can chime in if he's got something there, but we did standardize it all to a common lot size.

Yep. That's, yeah, as I recall, that was the case. So we'll add that as a completion of a different type. Then promoting ARD subdivisions by allowing them as of right. That was generally believed to have been completed, including low impact development and future developments. That would, you know, be, I believe, probably a regulatory change that would sort of encourage that sort of design to be incorporated into site planning. And again, most were believed that yeah. They're uncertain or believed that it had been done. And then the last is consider requiring a special permit for conventional subdivision designs, which I suppose would then thereby sort of disincentivize conventional subdivision in favor of conservation or or low impact subdivision.
And I do think that our current regulations require low impact design. We
looked at that pretty hard when we were looking at the new senior community center. So,

John, and and just to be clear, the current regulations. So, what what it is is all residential development is under the Andover Rural Design District. The anything any if you start with any piece of property that's bigger than 10 acres, the as of right subdivision is a conservation subdivision, which is 30,000 square foot lots with 40% designated to open space. By special permit, you can do a conventional subdivision, but you have to prepare a plan both ways and convince the commission why a conventional, you know, subdivision would work better on your particular site. Right. Okay. So I would say that's a check. Definitely. Is. Yeah. That that that has been done precisely as you describe it.

Okay. That's great. All right. So the next one I'm sorry, Jed, you want to skip through the natural resources? Yes. Yeah. We'll cover that next time when we got those folks here. So here we're going on. This is chapter nine, promoting and regulating commercial development. And let me scroll down. This is okay.

Space. Space. Okay. A couple more. Sorry. So business retention and business attraction. People generally Nobody believed that was complete, although obviously business retention and business attraction are ongoing matters. Correct. So people believed it to be, you know, important as an ongoing thing, which I think is certainly fair. That's not something you'd wanna leave off.
I mean, it's definitely our ongoing charge with economic development to continue working on that.

Okay, so the next one is further streamline development process and consider tax abatement ordinances. There was a lot of confusion. Some people thought it wasn't done, but still relevant. Others thought it was not done but also not particularly a major priority. And then there was a little uncertainty. So we kind of had mixed feelings about this. And I'll pause a little bit for comment, but we'll move on in the interest of time. If someone has something to say, please feel free to jump in. Well, I think Eric's comments on the tax abatement
